110  THE SAVOY MALE AND FEMALE COLLEGE

The "Suspension of Rules"—Social visits between young gentlemen and ladies were not always clandestine, however. On special occasions there was a general standing announcement of the "suspension of the rules"—and that announcement was more stirring to the students than the making of dates. For some occasions, such as for "exhibitions" and scheduled holidays, the suspension of rules was anticipated for some time in advance. Sometimes, for unexpected occasions, the announcement was a partial surprise, and as a consequence all the more exciting. The college paper tells of one instance when the rule had been suspended: man had successfully presented a request for "suspension of rules" and this produced this result:

The young girls were so hilarious over the suspension of the rules that as I hurried past I almost felt the suspension of the rules! I met B. M. and little M. is a small man in stature; they wanted me to play a little too; so I went into the situation with all my heart. But something happened: I was brought up short.

Date making was a formal affair. The gentleman sent his "compliments" (by which name the whole written message was called) to the young lady, a carefully worded note asking her company for the occasion. In the note book, the young lady had her carefully phrased note accepting or rejecting the date. In one of her note books still in existence, the date, if other demands that means of transportation than walking, and the young gentleman had to provide it; the two literary societies kept rosters of the dates by the two lively stables of Savoy.

The Magnified Importance of the First Date—A boy's first date, translated from reminiscence, can be a little something must go wrong, and little things assume large proportions in the mind of a young man. It is reported to Mr. Barlow McMahon, that the particular case of first-date difficulties of a Savoy College student is reported by Mr. Barlow McMahon as follows. The lines are from a Platonian Messenger:

IDENTITY

She was a handsome visitor,
And he was a bright young Prof.!
They met that morn to say farewell
For she was going off—

²Personal letter from Miss M. S. (Shel) Noel) Parks, Denton, Texas, July 15, 1938.
